http://www.indiagazette.com/news/2792100.text: President Droupadi Murmu arrives in New Delhi after concluding historic three-nation European visit ANI 26 Jul 2026, 06:28 GMT+10 New Delhi [India], July 26 (ANI): President Droupadi Murmu on Sunday arrived in New Delhi after concluding her historic three-nation visit to Eastern Europe. Noting her arrival, Rashtrapati Bhavan wrote in a post on X, 'President Droupadi Murmu arrived in Delhi after completing her State visits to Moldova, North Macedonia and Romania.' https://x.com/rashtrapatibhvn/status/2081156622064537913 The President concluded her landmark visits on Saturday, securing key diplomatic breakthroughs with Moldova, North Macedonia, and Romania to significantly bolster bilateral ties across trade, defence, tourism, and core economic sectors. The diplomatic engagement marked several historic milestones, establishing Murmu as the first Indian head of state to visit both Moldova and North Macedonia. Her arrival in Romania also marked the first visit by an Indian president to the Eastern European nation in over three decades. During the final leg of her visit to Romania, which began on July 23, New Delhi and Bucharest agreed to double their trade volume over the next three years while deepening defence cooperation and allied strategic areas. President Murmu held comprehensive talks on bilateral relations with Romanian President Nicusor Dan and separately engaged with Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan. She also addressed the India-Romania Business Forum in Bucharest on Friday and interacted with members of the India-Romania Parliamentary Friendship Group. Recognising her public leadership and international outreach, the Bucharest University of Economic Studies conferred an honorary doctorate upon President Murmu. The 'Doctor Honoris Causa' represents the institution's highest academic distinction, awarded to eminent personalities for exceptional contributions to academia, public service and international cooperation. Before she departed for the airport on Saturday, President Murmu met with members of the Indian diaspora. Romania currently hosts over 13,500 Indian nationals, including approximately 10,000 workers. Earlier, during her visit to North Macedonia from July 21 to 22, President Murmu held bilateral discussions with President Gordana Sijanovska-Davkova, which were followed by delegation-level talks. Both nations resolved to double bilateral trade figures and identified joint opportunities in tourism, hospitality, and filmmaking. During her stay in Skopje, Murmu addressed the Assembly of North Macedonia and presided over the inaugural session of the India-North Macedonia Business Forum. The European visit commenced on July 20 in Moldova, where President Murmu held extensive talks with Moldovan President Maia Sandu, evaluating the entire spectrum of bilateral engagement. The two leaders agreed to intensify joint efforts across key sectors, including agriculture, logistics, infrastructure, healthcare, pharmaceuticals, renewable energy, and innovation. Russia could launch a "limited" attack on NATO soil within the next few years, according to a new report, adding fresh weight to assessments trickling out across the alliance about Moscow's ability to target its 32 members before they build up their militaries and are fractured by the United States' attitude toward Europe. The Kremlin may try to take a bite out of a NATO country by sending troops over its border or carrying out hybrid attacks such as cyber assaults, The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing U.S. intelligence analysis. The estimates put the timeline for these operations any time between fall 2026 and 2029. Read More on World While officials from NATO have long warned that Russia could seize a chunk of one of the Baltic states once its long-running war in Ukraine wraps up, intelligence agencies don't always agree on exactly when Moscow would be ready to escalate from hybrid operations already taking place to military ones against alliance territory. But a small-scale Russian land-grab, if it happened as early as the next few months, would come before many NATO militaries have pulled through on their pledges to surge defense spending and beef up their armed forces. ... The U.S. previously believed Russian President Vladimir Putin wouldn't launch an attack on NATO while bogged down in Ukraine, contending with the human toll on the eastern front lines and the economic strain of the conflict. This has now changed because of Ukraine's recent success in targeting Russia's oil and commercial sites, unnamed U.S. officials told the Journal . Russia has repeatedly denied planning to attack NATO territory, and dismissed the claims as "nonsense." A large-scale attack on NATO is extremely unlikely, with Russia expected to instead consider a smaller, probing military operation against one of the Baltic states or Poland. For this type of incursion, Russia wouldn't need a high number of troops, analysts say; Moscow would just require a small force that takes a sliver of land, but ultimately doesn't inspire all of NATO—including the U.S. and the western European nations—to strike back overwhelmingly. Their failure to do so, they say, would spell the end of NATO's credibility and delight the Kremlin. NATO states are bound by Article 5 of the alliance's founding treaty, which commits all members to the defense of another NATO country if they're attacked. But it's less clear how the 32 members would respond to hybrid or "gray zone" tactics, including sabotage of critical infrastructure, or to Russian soldiers seizing a small chunk of strategically unimportant territory over its borders. Many in Europe worry NATO's unity has been frayed by President Donald Trump and his administration, which could embolden Putin to believe this White House—which will be in power throughout the period outlined in the Journal's report—wouldn't come to the aid of Eastern Europe if attacked. The U.S. has berated Europe and Canada for low defense spending and an overreliance on American forces, lathering these countries with disdain while warming relations with the Kremlin. Related Story NATO Forced To Repeatedly Scramble Fighter Jets To Intercept Russian Planes The Pentagon is currently reviewing how many troops it deploys in Europe, while NATO members on the continent work out how to plug the gaps American forces may leave in their defenses if they're ripped away—all while largely insisting the U.S. is still fully committed to the continent. "We are always thinking through and preparing for any number of scenarios," said NATO spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell. "NATO is watching and we are ready to deter and defend as necessary, which we continue to demonstrate." But with NATO not yet rearmed, questions over the U.S.'s desire to commit to defending strips of Eastern Europe under Trump in doubt and burgeoning fears over U.S. munitions stocks after months of war with Iran, the factors that previously put Putin off "aren't deterring him as much any more," said Jim Townsend, a former Pentagon official. So, what are the options for Russia, should it attempt a "limited" attack? Small Land Grab This is generally seen as the realistic worst-case scenario. But it becomes increasingly likely the more time passes, the U.S. officials said. Some analysts say that if Russia did move to take part of NATO territory, it would probably amass soldiers close to Estonia, Latvia or Lithuania's eastern borders. Some would likely be deployed to confuse NATO forces monitoring where Russia may try to push through, disguising the true targets and forcing NATO to spread its defenses. When Russian soldiers cross the border, they'd be accompanied by electronic warfare systems to confuse NATO communications and navigation, and cyber onslaughts. Once they hold a piece of land, Moscow would quickly populate the area with air defenses that could shoot down NATO aircraft that skirted within range to strike Russian forces, some experts predict. NATO is actively rehearsing for this scenario to happen in the next four years. The Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC), which would be some of the very first NATO troops deployed if Russian tanks were poised to enter the Baltic states, war-gamed a Russian invasion of these three countries in 2030 in May this year. NATO says it picked 2030 because that's when the threat from Russia will be "most acute." But Russia is already building an entirely new garrison to house up to 6,000 soldiers in Petrozavodsk, a city in Russia's northwest near Finland, the country's YLE broadcaster reported in June. Russian media separately reported Russia was constructing "more than 50 facilities from scratch" in the Karelia region bordering Finland. Another scenario could be operations around the Suwałki Gap, said Ed Arnold, a senior adviser for defense with The D Group organization of business leaders and experts. A small strip of land close to the Polish-Lithuanian border that links Belarus to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, the Suwałki Gap is a constant, rumbling concern in Eastern Europe. The 40-mile Suwałki Gap has been intermittently described as NATO's weak point and the alliance's most fortified boundary. Russian soldiers could push into the gap from Kaliningrad or from Belarus, sweeping outward and broadening up the corridor by eating into Polish and Lithuanian territory, Arnold told Newsweek . But it wouldn't need to be an attack made up of bloated numbers of Russian soldiers. A war-game run by German newspaper Die Welt in December, simulating a Russian incursion into Lithuania in October 2026, found that with just 15,000 troops, Russia was able to seize the Lithuanian city of Marijampole from the Suwałki Gap. In the war-game, the U.S. didn't invoke Article 5, and Germany dithered, ultimately leaving Russia victorious in its territorial snatch and in its goal of undermining NATO. Putin "knows he can't do NATO militarily, but he can do it politically," Arnold said. Hybrid Attacks "Hybrid attacks" is a catch-all term for operations that stop short of open fighting, like cyberattacks, information campaigns, arson incidents or the targeting of vulnerable infrastructure, such as undersea cables. NATO says Russia has been waging a hybrid war with the alliance for years. "We call on Russia to stop these destabilising activities," the alliance said in a statement last month after what it called "persistent malicious cyber activities" from Moscow. And at least 13 cables under the Baltic Sea were damaged between fall 2023 and the start of 2025. The overwhelming majority of the world’s data travels via undersea cables, effectively underpinning much of normal daily life. Targeting these cables can have huge military and civilian implications and give an adversary a major advantage for carrying out other operations. German authorities said on Wednesday they had found a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, a major military nexus and logistics hub in the east of the country. German police were deployed to dispose of the device, which they said was found near planes belonging to Ukraine's Antonov Airlines. Much of the aid for Ukraine is routed through Leipzig, as well as many NATO operations. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said officials were treating the incident as a "professional hybrid threat" and investigating whether it was set up by a foreign power. In late 2024, it emerged that Western intelligence officials suspected Russia of plotting to put incendiary devices aboard cargo planes, including aircraft bound for the U.S. Four packages were sent from Lithuania to the United Kingdom and Poland in July 2024, one of which caught fire just before it was loaded onto an aircraft in Leipzig. Another caught fire in a warehouse in the U.K., and a third was set ablaze on a truck in Poland. Moscow has been linked to a string of arson attacks on properties connected to then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer, with two people thought to be in touch with Russian intelligence sentenced in the U.K. in June. "We reject any attempt to associate Russia or its foreign ministry with unlawful activities," the Russian Embassy in the U.K. said at the time. "The speed, scale and intensity of hybrid threats have increased in recent years," NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in January. "Being prepared to prevent, counter and respond to hybrid attacks, whether by state or non-state actors, is a top priority for NATO." Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images US immigration US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms Associated Press Mon 19 Oct 2026 18.34 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 18.43 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday. Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”. Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”. The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status. The DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect. The decision marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long. Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a non-profit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the US, described the government’s announcement as “last-minute patches”. It is a “bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue,” he said. “It’s time for US to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people,” Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine. Andrew Arthur, a national-security and immigration expert at the Center for Immigration Studies, a Washington thinktank that favors lower immigration, said the government will eventually decide but faces no deadline. Until then, nothing changes, he said. “It’s simply going to be an extension until it is a termination,” he said. “It’s beyond cavil that both Sudan and Ukraine are experiencing ongoing armed conflict, and therefore the secretary is well within his authority to continue TPS for each of them.” The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorians whose TPS was set to expire on 9 September. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the US. Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia. Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when the DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026. The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive US administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation. Monday’s decision comes two weeks before the midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.
